title: Welcome to the house
body: Welcome to the house. Letters come to this desk, and you answer them. You send our people out to buy where goods are cheap and sell where they are dear. At the end, the house is judged on its money, its good name, the people who came home, and what you learned.

choices.label: Let's begin
choices.result: Sabir opens the ledger. The first letters are already on the desk.

note: Ibn Battuta wrote that Cairo surged like the waves of the sea. Merchants there had long run their trade by letter, with agents and friends in other cities.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 52 to 53; the sultan and the city
the Geniza letters, mostly 950 to 1250: merchants and their agents writing to each other

title: Welcome to the house
body: Welcome to the house I rented you. Letters come to this desk, and you answer them. You send people out to buy where goods are cheap and sell where they are dear. At the end, the house is judged on its money, its good name, the people who came home, and what you learned.

choices.label: Let's begin
choices.result: Nabil hands you the keys. The first letters are already on the desk.

note: Ibn Battuta wrote that Cairo surged like the waves of the sea. Merchants there had long run their trade by letter, with agents and friends in other cities.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 52 to 53; the sultan and the city
the Geniza letters, mostly 950 to 1250: merchants and their agents writing to each other

title: Look after a friend's son
body: Girgis is a merchant in Damascus. He writes that his partner's son is coming to Cairo to learn the trade. He asks you to find the boy a place and keep an eye on him.

choices.label: Take the boy in
choices.hint: Girgis will owe you a favour.

choices.label: Say you cannot
choices.hint: Girgis will find someone else.

note: Merchants had long done each other favours and expected the same.

sources.at: p. 316; the friend who serves "there" for the friend who serves "here"
merchants asking correspondents to look after others, as Edwards and Ogilvie (2008), p. 18 report

title: A gift, and a nephew
body: Ilyas is a merchant in Syria. He sends your house two loads of glass as a gift. He asks you to take his nephew Tadros as an agent. Tadros is careful, and good with figures.

choices.label: Take Tadros and keep the glass
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars to take him on. Ilyas will owe you.

choices.label: Keep the glass and find Tadros a place with a friend
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars, and the friend pays you 9 in thanks. Ilyas will notice.

choices.label: Send the gift back with thanks
choices.hint: You owe nothing, and you gain 2 dinars in two seasons. Ilyas will think it odd.

note: In a letter of the Geniza papers one merchant tells another: he serves there and I serve here. Merchants in different cities did each other favours and expected the same.

sources.at: p. 316; he serves there and I serve here

title: A gift meant for Samir
body: Samir is home from {to}. A buyer Samir met there was pleased to deal with him. He sends 7 dinars to your desk as a gift for the man who found him. The gift came to the house, but it was meant for Samir.

choices.label: Give Samir the 7 dinars
choices.hint: It costs you nothing you had. Samir will tell others.

choices.label: Give Samir three and keep four
choices.hint: You gain 4 dinars. Samir shrugs.

choices.label: Keep it for the house
choices.hint: You gain 7 dinars. Samir is not told.

note: In the Geniza papers a commission was paid for a special service and not for the friendship. A merchant who did a favour was repaid by a favour.

sources.at: p. 316; the commission paid for a special service, and the favour repaid by a favour

title: Tadros is home from {to}
body: Tadros is home from {to}. Ilyas has written to ask how he behaved. Tadros asks if the house will keep him on, and if it will write back to his uncle.

choices.label: Keep him on and write well of him
choices.hint: It costs a clerk's time, 2 in two seasons. Ilyas will be glad.

choices.label: Thank him and let him return to his uncle
choices.hint: Ilyas gets his nephew back.

note: In a letter of the Geniza papers one merchant tells another: he serves there and I serve here. Merchants in different cities did each other favours and expected the same.

sources.at: p. 316; he serves there and I serve here

title: A tomb that feeds travellers
body: Bahram has come to Cairo from Samarkand, a city far to the east. Outside his town stands a tomb, and visitors leave gifts there. The gifts feed travellers who stay at the hospice beside it, a guest house for people on the road. Bahram asks if your house will give a little too.

choices.label: Send a small gift to the hospice
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. Travellers from the east will speak well of your house.

choices.label: Ask Bahram to carry a letter east
choices.hint: It costs 1 dinar now. Your partners hear from you, and Bahram asks for nothing more.

choices.label: Give nothing
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Bahram tells people your house is careful with money, not kind.

note: In 1333 the traveller Ibn Battuta saw people bring animals and money to the tomb of Qutham, outside Samarkand. The gifts fed travellers and paid the staff of the hospice.

title: A room for a merchant
body: Kamal has sailed to Aden from Calicut. Great ships come to Aden from India, and merchants of India and of Egypt live there. Kamal asks for a room in your warehouse.

choices.label: Give him a room
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. Kamal remembers a kind house when he trades again.

choices.label: Charge him rent
choices.hint: He pays you 3 dinars now. He finds the rent high, and word gets round.

note: Ibn Battuta wrote that Aden was the port of the merchants of India. Great ships came there from Cambay, Quilon, Calicut and other places, and merchants from India and Egypt lived there.

sources.at: vol. 2, p. 372 (the port of the merchants of India)

title: Water has a price
body: Tahir lives in Hormuz, on an island with no springs. The water comes in skins from far away, so it has a price. He asks what your people will pay.

choices.label: Pay his price
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. Tahir is glad of your custom.

choices.label: Bring your own water
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. It is dearer, but partners see you are ready.

choices.label: Move on
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Tahir shrugs, and word gets round.

note: On the island of Hormuz, water had a price. It came from springs and cisterns some way from the city, carried in waterskins on people's backs and then by boat.

title: A gift for the customs masters
body: A trader at Pera says it is the custom to honour the customs masters with a gift. Customs are taxes on goods. The gift goes to the masters, their clerks and their interpreters.

choices.label: Send gifts to the masters and their clerks
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. Your goods are counted at less than their worth, and the court hears of your manners.

choices.label: Send a gift of cloth only
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now. The clerks are pleased, and partners hear of it.

choices.label: Send nothing
choices.hint: It costs nothing now and 2 dinars in two seasons, because your goods are counted at full worth.

note: Pegolotti advised merchants to give the customs masters a gift, and their clerks something too. Then, he said, they pass you politely and count your goods at less than they are worth.
